purpose: Test source-first transformation from reusable corpus evidence into structured subject knowledge without creating learner-facing copy.

aiRole: map supported knowledge to AQA named requirements
aiMustNot: treat AQA wording as reusable teaching prose

coreConcepts: Conformity is a change in behaviour or expressed judgement in response to real or perceived group pressure.
Compliance is an outward response to a request or social pressure and does not necessarily imply private agreement.
Internalisation involves adopting a norm or position from an internal motive rather than merely responding to external monitoring or sanction.

Normative social influence reflects concern with social approval or rejection; informational social influence reflects reliance on others as evidence about what is correct, especially when the situation is uncertain.
Asch-style conformity changes with majority size and unanimity; the presence of a dissenter can sharply reduce conformity.
More difficult or ambiguous judgement tasks tend to increase informational dependence and can increase conformity.
Milgram's obedience studies show that ordinary participants can follow instructions from an authority even when the instructed action appears harmful.
Situational conditions alter obedience: proximity to the learner and the perceived authority/status of the setting affect compliance with instructions.

The agentic-state account proposes that people may define themselves as carrying out an authority's wishes rather than acting fully autonomously, reducing experienced personal responsibility; modern evidence also gives reasons not to treat this as a complete explanation.
Legitimacy of authority concerns whether an authority is perceived as proper and entitled to influence behaviour; perceived legitimacy can support voluntary acceptance of authority.
Uniforms and other authority-linked symbols can act as status and authority cues and can increase compliance relative to non-authority signals.

Authoritarian-disposition accounts emphasise submission to established leaders, aggression toward norm violators and conventionalism as traits or attitudes relevant to obedience, but contemporary evidence cautions against treating authoritarianism as a fixed or sufficient cause.
structuredKnowledge.alignmentCaution: The exact AQA packaging of agentic state, legitimacy, uniform and authoritarian personality is an alignment choice. The reusable sources provide the underlying subject knowledge; Revision authors the mapping rather than copying AQA prose.

coreConcepts: Locus of control concerns whether people tend to attribute outcomes mainly to their own actions or to external forces.
A stronger internal locus of control is associated with lower conformity than a stronger external locus of control in the inspected open evidence, although context matters.
Social support can reduce conformity: in Asch-style settings, the presence of another person who dissents from the majority can sharply reduce conformity by breaking unanimity.
Resistance to social influence can therefore be supported both by personal agency-related tendencies and by evidence that others are willing to resist the majority.
structuredKnowledge.alignmentCaution: The final sentence is Revision-authored synthesis of two independently supported mechanisms; it should not be represented as a direct quotation or single-study finding.

supports: internal locus of control associated with lower conformity
external locus associated with higher conformity

coreConcepts: Minority influence depends strongly on the behavioural style of the minority rather than simply its size.
Consistency over time and internal agreement make a minority position appear stable and deliberate.
Commitment or investment in a position can signal that the minority view is sincerely held rather than opportunistic.
Influence is weakened when consistency becomes rigidity; some openness and flexibility can make a minority more persuasive while preserving a coherent position.

manualInterventions: Official AQA scope checked and paraphrased into stable requirement IDs.
Reusable-source licences were verified before evidence was counted.
Convenient non-commercial sources were rejected even where they closely matched AQA terminology.
Claims were separated into direct source support, Revision-authored alignment/synthesis and explicit cautions.
AI-assisted structuring and independent phrasing were used only after the subject evidence existed.
sliceMetrics.elapsedWorkingTime: not reliably measurable retrospectively across multi-chat governed execution

works: A representative AQA topic can be made source-complete using commercially reusable material without buying a textbook or generating unsupported subject knowledge.
Broad OER plus targeted open research is sufficient to close both small and medium AQA-specific bridges in this slice.
AI is useful as a low-cost structuring, reconciliation and phrasing layer after evidence discovery rather than as the primary source of truth.
Rights and provenance can remain attached at requirement level without adopting the existing Content Factory orchestration.
remainingUncertainty: Whether the same economics hold across the 47 option requirements, especially Forensic Psychology.
Whether a complete Foundation representation for a more specialist topic remains equally source-light.
Learner-facing educational quality has not been tested in this prototype slice.
